content: Then all Israel gathered themselves to David to Hebron, saying, “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh. {{v:2}} In times past, even when Saul was king, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. The LORD your God said to you, ‘You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over my people Israel.’” {{v:3}} So all the elders of Israel came to the king to Hebron; and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD. They anointed David king over Israel, according to the LORD’s word by Samuel.

facets.evidence: inferring that the kinship formula establishes an 'organic union' framing his reign requires reading the Genesis 2:23 echo and political theology into the declaration
facets.text: Israel's declaration to David, "we are your bone and your flesh" (echoing Genesis 2:23), frames the king as bound to the people by shared kinship rather than as an external ruler, establishing his reign as an organic union with all Israel.
facets.question: Why do the Israelites tell David that he is their own bone and flesh?
facets.working_text: When all Israel gathers to David at Hebron, they say, "Behold, we are your bone and your flesh." This echoes Adam's cry over Eve in Genesis 2:23 and expresses that the king is not a foreign overlord but one drawn from the people's own kinship. The Chronicler presents David's kingship as an organic union with the whole people—all Israel, not merely Judah—rather than a conquest imposed from outside. This bodily solidarity anticipates the way Christ, the Son of David, shares our flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14) so as to be head of a people who are his own body.

facets.evidence: NT typological tradition: John 10:11 and Ezekiel 34:23 read David's shepherd-kingship as fulfilled in Christ the Good Shepherd
facets.text: God's word naming David "shepherd" and "prince" over Israel defines kingship as pastoral care for the people rather than domination, a shepherd-king ideal fulfilled in Christ the Good Shepherd (John 10:11, Ezekiel 34:23).
facets.question: What does it mean that God appointed David to be a shepherd over Israel?
facets.working_text: The people recall that even under Saul it was David who "led out and brought in Israel," a military idiom for a shepherd-leader who goes before the flock in battle and returns it safely. They ground his claim not in ambition but in his proven service and, decisively, in the LORD's own word: "You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over my people Israel." The shepherd image defines Israelite kingship as pastoral care rather than domination, and it is fulfilled in Jesus the Good Shepherd (John 10:11) and the shepherd-ruler foretold in Ezekiel 34:23 and Micah 5:2–4.

facets.evidence: inferring that the covenant anticipates 2 Samuel 7 and frames monarchy as mutual bond rather than seizure of power goes beyond what the passage states
facets.text: David makes a covenant with the elders "before the LORD" prior to his anointing, presenting the monarchy as a mutual, God-witnessed bond between king and people rather than a seizure of power, anticipating the Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7.
facets.question: Why did David make a covenant with the elders before becoming king?
facets.working_text: David does not simply seize the throne; he "made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD" before being anointed king. The Chronicler frames the monarchy as covenantal and mutual, enacted in God's presence, binding king and people together under divine witness. This covenant-making foreshadows the fuller Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7 and 1 Chronicles 17, and it reflects the biblical pattern that legitimate authority is bound by obligations before God rather than being merely a transfer of power.

facets.evidence: They anointed David king over Israel, according to the LORD's word by Samuel.
facets.text: David's anointing by all Israel fulfills "the LORD's word by Samuel" (1 Samuel 16), showing that the people's acclamation ratifies rather than creates the kingship, which rests on God's prior prophetic election.
facets.question: How does David's coronation fulfill what the prophet Samuel had earlier declared?
facets.working_text: The anointing of David is done "according to the LORD's word by Samuel," so that this public acclamation at Hebron merely ratifies what God had already decreed through the prophet at Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16). The Chronicler shows that the people's consent and the prophetic word converge: human choice does not create the king but recognizes God's prior election. This union of divine election and communal acclamation reveals that true authority in Israel flows from God's initiative confirmed through his prophets.

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: This passage narrates the anointing of David as king over all Israel at Hebron, grounding his monarchy in kinship solidarity, divine commission, covenantal obligation, and prophetic fulfillment, and serves as a key text for Davidic kingship, messianic typology, and the theology of covenant.

[scriptural/doctrinal | inferential]: The tribes' declaration of shared bone and flesh with David — echoing the language of Genesis 2:23 — presents the Israelite monarchy not as an imposition by an outside ruler but as an intrinsic union rooted in common humanity and kinship, making David's authority an expression of solidarity with the people he governs.

[typological/doctrinal | settled]: God's prophetic designation of David as "shepherd" and "prince" transforms the concept of royal power into an office of pastoral stewardship — a model of servant leadership over the flock of Israel that Christian tradition reads as a type of Christ the Good Shepherd (John 10:11) and the messianic ruler promised in Ezekiel 34:23.

[historical/doctrinal | inferential]: Before the anointing takes place, David formalizes a covenant with the elders of Israel in the presence of God, signaling that Davidic kingship is constituted by mutual, divinely witnessed obligation between ruler and people rather than by conquest or unilateral claim, and pointing forward to the fuller Davidic covenant established in 2 Samuel 7.

[scriptural/doctrinal | explicit]: The narrator explicitly ties David's coronation to the prophetic word spoken through Samuel (1 Samuel 16), making clear that the assembly's acclamation ratifies a divine election already decreed — the people confirm what God had predetermined, underscoring prophetic fulfillment and divine sovereignty in the origin of the Davidic dynasty.
